name: Copper
lede: Copper is the reddish-brown orange of the metal, named after Cyprus; the strange thing is that the red metal has given painters almost nothing red, and instead most of the blues and greens of the ancient and medieval paintbox.

sections.title: The red metal and its name
sections.body:
As a color, copper simply means the color of the metal, and the metal's English name goes back to Cyprus [1]. The Latin prefix *cupri-* gives the formal adjective *cupreous*, which Paterson defines as the reddish brown of copper [1]. St Clair describes the color as a reddish, rosy gold, and notes that for hair the word means something hotter, a fiery orange [7]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates copper as a color name to 1594, and the nearest ISCC-NBS category to this swatch is brownish orange [41].

The swatch on this page is the metal's average color, a warm brown-orange [41]. A flat screen cannot show shine, so it stands in for polished copper the way a photograph of a coin does. Other systems disagree on how light and pink it should be: the Crayola crayon called [[copper-crayola|Copper]] and our library's [[copper-red]] both sit about 13 units away, and [[copper-penny]] about 18 [41].

Copper was also a standard reference for naturalists. The color lists that grew out of Abraham Werner's mineral scale, from 1774 to 1821, include a copper red, and Richard Kirwan's 1794 list added a copper yellow [36][35]. Baty records the objection that such names only work for someone who has seen the object [37]. Copper is a moving target even then, because the metal itself changes color.

sections.title: From rose to green
sections.body:
Left outdoors, copper and its alloy bronze grow a green crust when oxygen, water, carbon dioxide or sulfur reach them [8]. The Statue of Liberty, dedicated in 1886, is made of copper and was first brown; weather and polluted air had turned it green by the early twentieth century [34]. St Clair puts the change at about thirty years, from rosy copper to full green [8].

That green, verdigris, gave its name to a color and a paint. Patrick Syme's 1814 color book used the green on copper as the mineral example for its [[verdigris-green]] [36]. Werner went further and argued that a mineral's color can hint at its chemistry: copper minerals, in his view, are mostly green or blue [35]. Baty presents this as Werner's argument, not a law, but the paintbox mostly bears it out [35].

sections.title: A red metal that paints blue and green
sections.body:
The Pigment Compendium calls copper pigments an extremely large group [21]. Almost all of them are blues and greens. The oldest is [[egyptian-blue]], made from about 2500 BC: one part lime, one part copper oxide and four parts quartz, fired at 800 to 900 degrees Celsius [12]. Ball calls it the oldest synthetic pigment [12]. Egyptian makers glazed small funerary figures and beads with copper blues and blue-greens, whose color was believed to protect the dead [25].

The natural copper ores azurite and [[malachite]] were dug from the same mines [24]. Azurite, a basic copper carbonate, was Dürer's usual blue, sold in Germany as mountain blue [13]. It leans green beside ultramarine, and it is less stable: Finlay notes that a robe of Michelangelo's Magdalene has faded from sea blue to olive [24]. Blue and green verditer, made by refiners, are the same copper carbonate-hydroxides in different proportions, and until the late eighteenth century nobody could control which one a batch would give [14].

Verdigris was made rather than mined. Vinegar, the strongest acid of antiquity, was enough to corrode copper into it, and Theophrastus gives the earliest account [12]. Later makers sealed copper sheets in pots with vinegar or sour wine for about two weeks and scraped off the green [8]; in Persia, Finlay reports, yogurt could stand in for the vinegar [23]. A late thirteenth-century recipe asks for the filings to steep three days or nine months, numbers Pastoureau reads as ritual rather than measurement [26]. The name means green of Greece in French, while German calls it *Grünspan*, Spanish green [8][5].

sections.title: Copper greens that turned brown
sections.body:
Roman wall painters already had copper greens. The painted garden in the Villa of Livia, from about 20 BC, uses malachite and artificial copper greens alongside green earths [27]. In the fifteenth century, painters working in oil added copper resinate, a green made by cooking verdigris with pine resin [14].

Many of those greens did not last. Jarman lists the dead copper greens of Venetian painting among famous pigment failures [44], and the brown foliage and hills of many Italian pictures of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries were once green [18]. Verdigris took the blame, but Ball reports that modern tests show little darkening in verdigris itself [18]. The likely culprit is copper resinate, whose resin breaks down in light [18]. Cennino Cennini called verdigris and lead white mortal enemies, yet tests show no harm in mixing them, and painters often did [18].

The real hazards were corrosion and chemistry. Pastoureau describes artificial copper greens attacking neighboring colors and even their supports [26]. Poussin still used a splendid but unstable oxidized-copper green, while Vermeer softened his copper green with honey [26]. Look closely at an old landscape with brown trees: the brown is often a green that changed, not the painter's choice.

sections.title: Arsenic greens
sections.body:
In 1775 the Swedish chemist Carl Scheele made copper arsenite, sold as [[scheele-s-green]] [15]. Two years later he privately worried that it was poisonous and should carry a warning [23]. In 1814 Wilhelm Sattler and Friedrich Russ at Schweinfurt found a brighter relative, copper aceto-arsenite, which the English called [[emerald-green]] [15].

Both went into wallpaper, cloth, artificial flowers and even sweets. By 1858 about a hundred square miles of British wallpaper used Scheele's green, and the death in 1861 of Matilda Scheurer, a nineteen-year-old maker of artificial flowers, helped end its use [9]. In 1862 the chemist August Hofmann found it in a ballroom head-dress, a use already banned in Bavaria [38].

Pastoureau goes further and suggests that damp green wallpaper at Longwood may have poisoned Napoleon [39]. That claim is unproven, and this article does not repeat it as fact.

sections.title: Copper in fire: glass
sections.body:
Glassmakers used copper for color from the start. In Egyptian glass, cobalt gave a deeper blue than copper, while greens came from iron or copper oxides, and those recipes passed almost unchanged to medieval cathedral windows [33]. Vitruvius described Roman blue glass made with soda and copper filings [24].

Copper is also two-faced in the furnace. Medieval glassmakers used the same copper oxide for red glass and for green, and the color depended on how long the glass was heated [2][28]. Around 1200, French window makers swapped cobalt for cheaper copper and manganese salts, which gave the murkier blues of windows such as the Sainte-Chapelle [25]. Aventurine, an Italian invention, is brown glass full of sparkling flecks of copper or gold [6].

sections.title: The rare copper reds
sections.body:
The metal's own color is hard to find in a paintbox. The nineteenth-century writer Salter listed only two copper reds: copper oxide, the mineral cuprite, and turacine [21]. Turacine is an organo-copper compound supposedly drawn from the feathers of the turaco, an African bird [22]. Salter dismissed it as a mere curiosity, because an entire plumage yields no more than three grains of it [22].

The browns came closer. Paterson lists Hatchett's brown, also sold as Roman brown and Florentine brown, as a copper color; the Pigment Compendium identifies it as a copper iron cyanide, copper hexacyanoferrate [4][45]. [[copper-brown]] in our library is far darker than the metal, about 24 units away [41].

sections.title: Plates, presses and a modern blue
sections.body:
Copper shaped the look of print. From about 1500, printers of books swapped their wood blocks for engraved copper plates, and textile printers soon did the same [16]. The black ink of Gutenberg's Bible of 1455 included iron or copper sulfate, which helped make the print impossible to scratch away [43]. Rembrandt painted some early pictures on gilded copper, a precious-material habit Gage finds old-fashioned [30].

The most important modern copper color is a blue. In 1928, chemists at Scottish Dyes noticed a blue contaminant while making another compound, and between 1935 and 1937 ICI developed its copper version, a deep turquoise [16]. Sold from 1935 as Monastral blue, copper phthalocyanine absorbs red and yellow light almost completely, which makes it close to an ideal cyan for color printing [17]. Its molecule has the same ring shape as chlorophyll, which holds magnesium, and haemoglobin, which holds iron [20]. The cyan in a color printer is, in this sense, a copper color too.

Artists also used the metal straight. Frank Stella painted early works with copper paint made to stop barnacles growing on boat hulls [19].

sections.title: Where to see copper
sections.body:
Copper is a color of glints as much as surfaces. The best indigo shows it: in 1610 William Finch listed what good indigo needed, and merchants tested a cake by scratching it for a coppery sheen [31]. Louisiana growers sold their best grade as *cuivre*, copper [32], and West African dyers beat indigo cloth with mallets to a coppery, bronzy shine [33]. Tilt a deeply dyed indigo cloth toward the light and look for that red-gold glint on the dark blue.

The color also belongs to hair. Elizabeth Siddal, the model for Millais's *Ophelia*, was famous for copper hair [11]. To the alchemists the metal belonged to Venus: a goldsmith's table from Strasbourg pairs Venus with green, copper and Friday [29]. Copper and green have been linked for as long as people have watched the metal age.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a screen color within six units of copper covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 685 works, about one in thirty-five [40]. It is most frequent in the 1300s and 1400s, at more than twice the archive's rate, and in the 1390s it appears in 5 of 25 dated works [40]. Where it covers the most canvas, it is mostly early Italian gold-ground panels: Paolo Veneziano's *[[art:nga-284|The Crucifixion]]* of about 1340 (46 per cent) and Duccio's *[[art:nga-282|The Calling of the Apostles Peter and Andrew]]* of 1308 (39 per cent) [40]. The earliest example is an Egyptian funerary papyrus of about 1069 BC [40].

This is the surprise. Copper pigments are blue and green, so the copper color in these paintings is almost certainly not copper: as photographed, aged gold leaf, warm grounds and yellowed varnish read as copper [40]. The same color covers 45 per cent of Van Gogh's *[[art:commons-Q26221149|Wheat Field with Sheaves]]* of 1888, which has no gold at all [40]. Inside paintings it is a light color: 67 per cent of the time it falls among the highlights, and almost never in shadow [40]. It shares canvases with [[ochre]] nearly 16 times more often than chance [40].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [40]. Our nearest named neighbors to the swatch are [[leather]] (3.6 units), [[tawny]] and India Spice (4.4) and Ochre (4.8) [41]. In Google Books the word, metal and color together, peaks in 1909 and has fallen to about 30 per cent of that level by 2000 [42].

questions.q: Copper is a reddish metal. What colors are most copper pigments?
Why are the trees in some fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Italian paintings brown?
choices: A copper green, often copper resinate, darkened over time
Green pigments were banned in Italy
questions.answer: A copper green, often copper resinate, darkened over time
